Four-year-old Yash woke screaming at the first crack of thunder. In the dark, Tarun sat on the bed and began stroking his back in slow circles, the way his own mother used to. Yash stiffened and wriggled away, crying harder. Tarun paused, stung for a second, then made himself watch instead of pushing on. By the phone torch he saw Yash reaching out, fingers spread. He took the small hand and held it still, no stroking. Yash's breathing slowed. His shoulders dropped. After a while he tugged Tarun's hand onto his head. "There," he mumbled. Tarun kept his palm resting there, not moving, until the rain softened and Yash's breath went long and even.

subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
passage:
Sunday night
Went to Afreen's house today, three days after her Ammi passed. The front room was full of aunties and the smell of agarbatti. Afreen was sitting on the floor mat, arms wrapped round her knees, not crying, just very still.
Every part of me wanted to throw my arms round her. But her shoulders were up by her ears, and people kept patting her and she kept flinching a little. So I sat down next to her, not touching, and said quietly, "Can I hug you, or would you rather I just sit?"
She said, "Just sit. For now."
So I sat. We didn't talk. After maybe half an hour she leaned sideways until her head was on my shoulder. I stayed still. I didn't want to break it.
Glad I asked first. Going back tomorrow with food.
Kashish

qa.a: Three days after her Ammi passed.

qa.a: Kashish felt a strong urge to hug but was concerned and careful, noticing Afreen's raised shoulders and small flinches when people patted her.

qa.a: It gave Afreen a real choice at a time when many people were touching her, so she could accept closeness when she was ready.

Usha set down her cup. She didn't say "Look on the bright side," and she didn't say "You're hiding something." She just waited, then asked quietly, "That's the funny version. How are you really?" Afreen's smile stayed for a second, then slipped. "Scared," she said. "Rent's due on the fifth, and I keep laughing so I don't cry on the train." Usha nodded. "Okay. Tell me the not-funny version. I've got all afternoon."

qa.q: How was Afreen laid off?
qa.a: By video call.

qa.q: What did Afreen's too-long laugh and folding napkin suggest?
qa.a: They hinted that behind the jokes Afreen felt scared and hurt; the humour might partly be real resilience, but it was also covering pain.

qa.q: What did Usha avoid saying, and why was her question better?
qa.a: She avoided 'look on the bright side' and 'you're hiding something', and gently asked how Afreen really was, which made room for the truth without accusing.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Afreen admitted being scared?
qa.a: Usha likely felt concerned but glad she had asked, and ready to listen for the whole afternoon.

grounding: Shows a young adult joking about a hard time, the laughter hiding fear, and a friend gently asking how she really is.

"Third time unlucky," Anand announced at dinner, dropping into his chair. "The examiners have now seen my handwriting more often than my own mother has."
Amma laughed. Usha didn't, quite. "You failed the accounts exam again?"
"By four marks. Four! I'm going to frame the result. 'Almost.'"
Usha studied him across the table. "Anand. Honestly. Is this funny-funny, or funny so you don't have to talk about it?"
He paused with a chapati halfway to his mouth. "Hm. Fair question." He chewed. "Honestly? It stung this morning. I sulked on the bus. But I've already booked the next attempt, and I know exactly which paper let me down. So... mostly funny-funny now."
"Okay." Usha passed the dal. "If it turns into the other kind, tell me."
"You'll be the first." He grinned. "After the frame shop."

qa.a: By four marks.

subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
passage: For about a month after the engagement ended, I was the funniest person in the office. I did a whole bit at lunch about returning the gold bangles to his mother "with a receipt". People laughed; I laughed louder. It felt like a shield. If I was making the jokes, nobody could feel sorry for me. Sunaina was the only one who didn't join in every time. One evening, when the floor had emptied, she stopped by my desk with two cups of tea. "Aparna, your jokes are good. But you laugh with your mouth and not your eyes these days. How are you really?" I opened my mouth to make another joke and couldn't. I cried for twenty minutes over that tea. She didn't try to fix anything. Looking back, the jokes weren't all fake; some of them did help. But I needed one person to ask.

qa.a: Two cups of tea.

subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
passage:
"He's safe?" Hansa's voice cracked into the phone. "You're sure? Okay. Okay."
She put the phone down on the table and made a sound Karthik had never heard from her, a huge, ragged sob. Then another. She folded over her knees.
"Hansa..." Karthik half rose, then stopped. "Is it Mohan?"
She nodded, gasping. "They found him. At the relief camp. Four days, Karthik. Four days I thought..."
"I know." He sat down beside her. "Cry. It's all right. Nobody's here but me."
"I can't stop."
"You don't have to yet."
She cried until her breath came in hiccups. Karthik fetched a glass of water and put it in her hands. "Small sips. Now breathe out slowly with me. Longer. Again."
Her shoulders began to drop. "I held it in for four days," she whispered. "At work, on the bus."
"That's why it all came at once. Want to call your mother now, together?"
"Yes."

qa.q: Where was Mohan found?
qa.a: At the relief camp.

qa.q: Why did Hansa cry so hard after the call?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed with relief after four days of fear she had held in at work and on the bus, so it all came out at once.

qa.q: How did Karthik help Hansa's body settle?
qa.a: He let her cry without hurrying her, then gave her water in small sips, breathed out slowly with her, and suggested calling her mother together.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Karthik to hear that sob?
qa.a: Karthik was probably startled and worried at first, having never heard that sound from her, then steady once he understood it was relief.

grounding: Shows an adult bawling with relief after long tension, allowed to cry in a safe place and then settling with water, slow breathing and support.

subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
passage: At Thatha's funeral I didn't cry once. I was the eldest grandchild; I organised the tent, the chairs, the priest, the food for two hundred people. Everyone said I was strong. A week later I was parked outside the office, and a song he used to hum came on the radio. I started crying so hard I couldn't see the steering wheel. Loud, ugly crying, the kind you'd never let anyone hear. I called Pema because she lived five minutes away. She didn't tell me to calm down. She got into the passenger seat, handed me a bottle of water and said, "Vijay, let it come. Then we'll breathe." When it slowed, she counted breaths with me, in for four, out for six. Afterwards I felt emptied out but lighter, like I'd put down a heavy bag carried all week. I think holding it in had made that week much longer.

qa.q: What came on the radio?
qa.a: A song Thatha used to hum.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after crying in the car?
qa.a: Vijay felt emptied out but lighter, as if a heavy bag carried all week had been put down.

qa.q: What helped Vijay's crying settle?
qa.a: Pema let the tears come without saying calm down, gave water, and then counted slow breaths, in for four and out for six.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt getting that call?
qa.a: Pema was likely worried and caring, coming quickly and staying calm so Vijay could fall apart safely.

grounding: A young adult recalls suppressing grief at a funeral, bawling a week later in a safe place, and settling with water, slow breathing and a friend.

subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
passage:
Hostel warden's note, 9 August. Written by Ayesha, warden, Nehru Nagar working men's hostel.
At about 8 pm, Jatin (Room 14) opened an email in the common room and began sobbing loudly. Several residents stood up, alarmed. I went over. Between sobs he told me it was the offer letter he had been waiting on for two years, after more than forty rejections. It was relief, not bad news.
I moved him to my office, away from the crowd, so he could cry without an audience. I did not ask him to stop. When it eased, I gave him a glass of water and asked him to breathe slowly with me for a minute. He then called his parents in Sikar and cried again, happily.
The residents were told only that he had good news.
Next step: I will check on him tomorrow morning, since a very big relief can leave a person shaky and tired for a while.

qa.q: How many rejections had Jatin had?
qa.a: More than forty rejections.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he began sobbing in the common room?
qa.a: Jatin was overwhelmed with relief after two years of waiting and rejections, though the loud sobbing made others think it was bad news.

qa.q: How did Ayesha help Jatin cry safely?
qa.a: She moved him to her office away from the crowd, let him cry without asking him to stop, then gave him water and breathed slowly with him.

qa.q: How did the other residents first see Jatin's sobbing?
qa.a: They were alarmed, assuming something terrible had happened, since loud sobbing can look the same for relief and for grief.

grounding: A warden notes a young adult bawling with relief after long tension and helping him cry safely, then settle with water and breathing.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: The client would arrive in fifteen minutes, and the manager had just torn into Rukmini's presentation in front of the whole open-plan floor. "Sloppy. Half these numbers don't match. Did you even check?" Rukmini felt her eyes sting and her chin wobble. There was no empty meeting room, no private corner, only rows of desks and people pretending not to look. She picked up her laptop and walked quickly to the stairwell. On the landing the tears came. She let them, pressing her back to the cool wall and breathing out slowly. The door opened; Sangeeta slipped in with a tissue and a bottle of water. "No speeches," she said. "Just this." Rukmini laughed shakily and wiped her face. After a minute she opened the laptop on her knees. "Slide four and slide seven don't match. I can fix both in ten minutes." She walked back in with the corrected deck and her chin steady.

qa.q: Which slides didn't match?
qa.a: Slide four and slide seven.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling after the manager's criticism?
qa.a: Rukmini felt hurt and embarrassed, eyes stinging and chin wobbling, in front of the whole floor with the client about to arrive.

qa.q: How did Rukmini manage the moment?
qa.a: She stepped out to the stairwell, let the tears come and breathed slowly, then returned with a concrete plan to fix the two slides.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta show kindness?
qa.a: Sangeeta followed with a tissue and water, kept it simple with 'no speeches', and gave Rukmini space to recover.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: Arnab had been on the call with the Mumbai client for forty minutes when it happened. "Frankly, this is amateur work," the client said, and hung up. Arnab stared at the black screen. His throat closed, and to his horror his eyes filled. In his first job a senior had told him, "Men don't cry in office." He blinked hard and gripped the desk, but a tear slid down anyway. Baljeet, at the next desk, saw. She didn't comment, and she didn't make a show of looking away. She just said, "Terrace? Five minutes?" Up there, among the water tanks and the neighbouring building's laundry, Arnab let his breath shudder out and wiped his face with his sleeve. "Sorry," he said. "Nothing to be sorry for," Baljeet said. When he had steadied, he said, "Okay. I'll ask for a list of exactly what they want changed, and do it by Friday." They went back down.

qa.q: How long had Arnab been on the call?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when his eyes filled?
qa.a: Arnab felt hurt by the harsh words and horrified at crying, remembering a senior saying men don't cry in office.

qa.q: What helped Arnab recover and move forward?
qa.a: A short break on the terrace to breathe and wipe his face, then a plan to ask exactly what the client wanted changed and deliver by Friday.

qa.q: How did Baljeet respond, and why was it kind?
qa.a: Baljeet didn't comment or stare, just offered five quiet minutes on the terrace and said there was nothing to be sorry for, letting him recover with dignity.

grounding: Shows a young professional tearing up after harsh words despite workplace norms, stepping out to breathe and returning with a plan, and a peer's kindness.

"...so the report can't go out like this, Naveen. The data section needs to be redone."
Naveen nodded. He opened his mouth to answer and found his eyes had filled. "Sorry. I... sorry."
Dolma pushed the tissue box across the desk. "No need. Take your time."
"I worked all weekend on it." His voice wobbled. "Can I step out for a couple of minutes?"
"Of course. The water cooler's free. Come back when you're ready."
He came back five minutes later, face washed, carrying a notepad.
"Better?" Dolma asked.
"Yes. Thanks. Can we go through exactly what's wrong in the data section? I'd like to fix it by Thursday."
"That's a good plan." She turned her screen toward him. "And Naveen, the structure is strong. It's only the data. I should have said that first."
He let out a breath. "That helps."

subtype: Supporting someone who is crying [Interpreting]
passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Anjali cried on my bed for an hour tonight. Her research proposal got rejected, the one she's spent eight months on, and her supervisor's email was two lines long.
My first instinct was to say, "Don't cry, it's not the end of the world," because I hate seeing her like that. I actually had my mouth open. Then I remembered how much I hated it when people told me to stop crying after Dadi died. It made my tears feel like a problem to fix.
So I passed her the tissue box and sat on the floor by the bed. After a while I asked, "Do you want me to listen, or distract you, or just be here?" She said, "Just be here. Maybe listen later."
Later she talked for ages. I mostly said "hmm". At the end she hugged me and said it helped.
Gurleen

qa.q: How long had Anjali spent on the research proposal?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when about to say 'Don't cry'?
qa.a: Gurleen felt upset and helpless seeing Anjali cry and wanted it to stop, before remembering how hurtful that had felt after Dadi died.

qa.q: Why was Gurleen's question to Anjali helpful?
qa.a: Asking whether Anjali wanted listening, distraction or company let her choose, respecting her control instead of treating the tears as a problem to fix.

qa.q: How did Anjali experience Gurleen's support?
qa.a: Anjali felt comforted enough to talk for ages later and said it helped, because she wasn't rushed or told to stop.

grounding: Shows a young adult resisting the urge to say stop, offering tissues and presence, and asking a crying friend what would help.

subtype: Supporting someone who is crying [Interpreting]
passage: The little post office in Bishnupur was about to close when Bidisha saw Leela sitting on the bench outside, crying into the end of her dupatta. The letter in her lap had a government stamp. Bidisha's first impulse was to say, "Arre, stop, people are looking." The postmaster was already peering out. Instead she sat down beside Leela, took a clean handkerchief from her bag, held it out and said nothing for a while. Leela's shoulders shook. A goat cart rattled past. Eventually Bidisha asked softly, "Do you want to tell me, or shall we just sit? Or should I walk you home?" Leela wiped her eyes. "My passport's delayed again. The hospital in Dubai won't hold the job past next month." She cried again, and Bidisha let her. When Leela was ready, Bidisha said, "Tomorrow I'll come with you to the passport office in the district town."

qa.q: Where was the hospital job?
qa.a: In Dubai.

qa.q: What was Bidisha's first impulse, and what does it show she felt?
qa.a: Bidisha felt awkward and self-conscious about people looking, and was tempted to tell Leela to stop.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do instead that helped?
qa.a: She sat beside Leela, offered a handkerchief, stayed quiet, then asked whether Leela wanted to talk, sit or be walked home, and later offered to go with her to the passport office.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Leela to be allowed to cry?
qa.a: Leela could let out her fear and disappointment without feeling rushed or ashamed, which made it easier to explain what was wrong.
